Des Moines areas and suburbs

Des Moines is Iowa's capital and the Polk County seat, built where the Des Moines and Raccoon Rivers meet. The part of the city south of County Line Road reaches into Warren County. The 2020 count was 214,133 residents in the city and 709,466 in the metro area, by a wide margin the biggest market in the state.

Sellers usually deal with a few distinct areas. Downtown and the East Village sit near the State Capitol on the east side of the Des Moines River. South of Grand is the older neighborhood around Salisbury House. Ringing the city are West Des Moines, Urbandale, Ankeny, Altoona, Clive, Johnston and Windsor Heights, and houses in those suburbs compete with city houses for the same buyers.

Most of the city belongs to the Des Moines Independent Community School District, the largest in Iowa, with East, Hoover, Lincoln, North and Roosevelt high schools plus an online campus. Small parts of Pleasant Hill and Windsor Heights fall in the district too. DART runs local, commuter and express buses.

Older houses and what buyers inspect

Des Moines began as Fort Des Moines in 1843 and became the capital in 1857, so many older streets date to the railroad and coal years. One block can hold houses from very different decades. Buyers of older houses usually ask for inspections of the plumbing, the wiring and the basement.

An owner who does not want to fund repairs before listing has another option, which is selling the house in its current condition. A cash buyer looks at the same plumbing, wiring and basement but prices what it finds instead of sending you a repair list.

Flood history near the rivers

Des Moines has flooded repeatedly, and buyers and lenders ask about it. A flood destroyed much of the early town in May 1851. The Great Flood of 1993 put the Des Moines Water Works under water on July 11. About 250,000 people had no running water for 12 days and no drinking water for 20.

A levee breached in June 2008. The Birdland neighborhood on the north side, along the Des Moines River, flooded in both 1993 and 2008. It now sits behind a rebuilt levee that cost $11 million, runs wider in many places and stands roughly 2 to 4 feet taller than the old one. Officials said tree growth had weakened the earlier levee and contributed to the 2008 failure, and that the new one does not remove flood risk.

  • Before choosing a closing date, find out from your insurance agent if the parcel is in a mapped flood zone.
  • Keep repair receipts and claim paperwork from past water damage, because buyers ask for them.
  • If the basement is damp, say so early. A cash buyer prices the condition in and does not need a repair list from you.

Rental certificates and code complaints

An owner who rents out a Des Moines house needs a rental certificate from the city. The Neighborhood Services Inspection Division inspects rentals and enforces the requirement when a house is rented without one.

The application asks that the owner's name match the Polk County Assessor's records. An owner who lives outside Polk County and its bordering counties must name an adult local management agent. The form is due back within 10 days, or the owner commits a municipal infraction, and a late form adds a $26 research fee.

The same division handles junk and debris, junk vehicles, illegal dumping, noise, graffiti and condemned buildings. It is at 602 Robert D. Ray Drive, 2nd floor. A vacant or inherited house that attracts complaints can pick up violations quickly.

  • Find the rental certificate if the house has been a rental.
  • Clear open code complaints, or tell a buyer about them in writing.
  • Check that the owner name on the deed matches the assessor record.

If the last day lands on a weekend or holiday, the deadline moves to the next business day. Late interest runs 1.5 percent per month, with a $1 minimum. A mailed payment counts as on time only with a postmark by the due date. You can also pay online at Iowa Tax and Tags. The Polk County Treasurer's office answers at 515-286-3060.

Unpaid taxes can be sold at the county's annual online tax sale, held each June. An owner who pays before the cutoff the day before the sale keeps the parcel off it.

At a sale, taxes are normally prorated. Either the buyer gets a credit for your share or you pay the treasurer directly at closing. Because Iowa taxes run a year behind, the September and March bills cover July 1 through June 30 of the prior year. Read the settlement statement closely.

On top of that comes the transfer tax, eighty cents for every $500 of value past the first $500, with a declaration of value filed alongside the recorded deed (Iowa Code 428A.1).

How does a cash sale work for a Des Moines house?

With no mortgage involved, a cash purchase has no lender appraisal and no loan approval holding it up. That can matter for houses with open permits, old systems or deferred repairs, which lenders sometimes will not approve.

  2. You receive a written offer that you can accept or turn down.
  3. Say yes, and a title company takes over the paperwork while taxes are settled at the closing table.
  4. The closing date is yours to choose, as long as the title work is done by then.

If the house is an inherited Des Moines property, a rental with tenants or a home behind on payments, tell us up front. Those situations change the paperwork, not the basic steps.

What to bring to the first conversation

You do not need a perfect file, but a few items save time. Bring the address and a rough account of what is wrong with the house. Add the latest tax statement, any rental certificate, notes from past flood or water repairs and the names that appear on the deed. If a lien, a payoff or a code notice is open, say so now so the title company can plan for it.

Then compare. A cash offer is one price for the house as it stands. A listing adds repair costs, showings, inspection credits and the time a buyer's loan takes. Put both on paper and choose the one that fits your date and your budget.

Selling a Des Moines rental or inherited house

Rentals and inherited houses are common reasons for a quick sale in Des Moines, and each has its own checklist. For a rental, find the city certificate, the current lease and any notice from the Neighborhood Services Inspection Division. Decide whether the tenant stays or leaves, and write the date down.

For an inherited house, make sure the deed names match the people who will sign. A house that sat empty may have attracted complaints about debris or a vehicle, so drive by and clear anything that could draw a notice before a buyer visits.

What counties does Des Moines sit in?

Des Moines is the seat of Polk County, and the part of the city south of County Line Road extends into Warren County. The Polk County Treasurer bills property tax for most Des Moines houses.

Does a Des Moines landlord need a rental certificate?

Yes. The city requires one, and its Neighborhood Services Inspection Division enforces the rule. The owner of record must return the application within 10 days or face a municipal infraction.

When are Polk County property taxes delinquent?

The first half is delinquent after September 30 and the second half after March 31. After that, interest accrues at 1.5 percent a month, with a $1 minimum.

Do Des Moines houses flood?

Some do. Low areas near the Des Moines and Raccoon Rivers flooded in 1851, 1993 and 2008, and the Birdland neighborhood on the north side now sits behind a rebuilt levee. Ask your insurer about your parcel.

Can I sell a Des Moines house with code violations?

Yes. A cash buyer can take the house as it stands. Open violations and liens are cleared by the title company at closing or dealt with in the contract.

Cedar Rapids layout and size

Cedar Rapids is the Linn County seat and the second most populous city in Iowa, with 137,710 residents at the 2020 count and 137,935 in mid-2025. It lies about 20 miles north of Iowa City and 128 miles northeast of Des Moines.

Addresses fall into four quadrants. The Cedar River divides east from west, and 1st Avenue (U.S. Route 151 Business) divides north from south. The city uses 14 ZIP codes, and downtown and Mays Island are in 52401. When you describe a house to anyone, give the quadrant and ZIP along with the street, because buyers search that way and the quadrant tells them which neighborhood and often which school district they are looking at.

Flood and derecho history

Two kinds of storm left their mark on Cedar Rapids housing, river water and wind. Buyers know both stories, so expect questions.

  • June 2008 flood: the Cedar River crested at a record 31.12 feet on June 13, well above the previous record of 20 feet. About 1,126 city blocks flooded, 7,749 properties were evacuated, 5,900 of them homes, and at least 1,300 properties were demolished.
  • September 2016 flood: the river reached 22 feet on September 27, the second highest crest on record against a flood stage of 12 feet. More than 5,000 homes were affected. The city had approved a $625 million, 20-year levee plan the year before.
  • August 10, 2020 derecho: winds of 60 to 80 mph, with gusts of 110 mph or more, knocked out power to about 95 percent of the city and damaged 20 schools.

If your house sits where water or wind did damage, a conventional buyer's inspector will look hard at the basement, the roof and the electrical system. Gather repair receipts and insurance paperwork before you talk price. A cash purchase lets you skip the back and forth over repair credits.

Neighborhoods and school districts

Twelve neighborhood associations are active in the city. Those nearest downtown include Wellington Heights, Oakhill Jackson and Moundview, and other named areas include Noelridge Park and Kenwood Park. Informal districts such as Czech Village, New Bohemia (NewBo), Kingston Village and Wilderness Estates also come up in listings.

Four school districts reach into the city, and your address decides which applies:

  • Cedar Rapids Community School District, with 15,589 students in 2023-24, 21 elementary schools, 6 middle schools and 5 high schools.
  • Linn-Mar Community School District, which covers part of the northeast quadrant.
  • College Community School District, which covers part of the southwest quadrant.
  • Marion Independent School District, which covers a portion of the city.

Families ask about the district before almost anything else, so check it for your street and state it accurately.

A landlord who is done managing a rental can sell it with tenants in place or after they move out. Ask the buyer whether the registration will carry over or has to be filed fresh, and call the city's housing inspections office to confirm before closing.

Each deed that goes through the Linn County Recorder carries a declaration of value, and most also carry a groundwater hazard statement. Iowa Code 558.69 lays out what the seller reports:

  • Private burial sites, underground storage tanks and known hazardous waste.
  • Solid waste disposal sites identified by the Department of Natural Resources.
  • Private sewage disposal systems, and whether they were inspected or are exempt at transfer.

At least one seller, or the seller's agent, signs the statement and the buyer gets a copy. You are responsible for the accuracy of your answers. After the 2008 flood, owners of older properties should dig through their records for any tank or well that was removed, capped or replaced, since an old note can settle a question quickly.

  3. If the offer works for you, pick a closing date and let a title company prepare the deed, declaration of value and groundwater statement.
  4. Close, and record the deed at the county.

You can say no to an offer at no cost. Compare it with what a listing would net after repairs, the wait for a buyer and the cost of carrying the house in the meantime.

Property taxes owed at the sale

Iowa property tax comes in two installments that turn delinquent on October 1 and April 1 under Iowa Code 445.37. Ask the Linn County Treasurer what is paid before the closing date, so the title company can divide the current bill between you and the buyer.

Bring the latest tax statement to the first conversation with a buyer. A paid-up house closes faster, and an installment that is already delinquent is something to raise early rather than at the closing table.

If the house is a rental, also bring the Certificate of Compliance and the latest registration receipt. Buyers who plan to keep renting want to know what carries over and what restarts, and the paperwork answers that in a minute.

Getting a house ready for a cash offer

You do not have to repair a Cedar Rapids house to sell it for cash, but a little preparation makes an offer more accurate. Walk through the basement first, since that is where flood and storm history show up most. Note any past water, any sump pump or drain work, and what the roof looked like after the 2020 derecho.

Next, write down what you know about wells, tanks and septic systems, because the groundwater statement asks for those facts. Then pull together the deed, any survey and the tenant lease if there is one. The more complete the picture you give a buyer, the closer the first offer will be to the final number.

It crested at a record 31.12 feet on June 13, 2008, against an earlier record of 20 feet. In all, 7,749 properties were evacuated, including 5,900 homes.

Yes. Rental housing needs a Certificate of Compliance to be occupied legally. Registration runs $50 a year for a single-family unit or condo, $60 for a duplex, and $42 plus $13 per unit for multi-family buildings.

Which school district is my Cedar Rapids house in?

It depends on the address. Cedar Rapids Community Schools covers most of the city, while Linn-Mar, College Community and Marion Independent each cover part of it.

Iowa Code 558.69 has the seller report wells, burial sites, underground tanks, hazardous waste, solid waste disposal sites and private sewage systems on a groundwater hazard statement filed with the deed.

Davenport and the Quad Cities

Davenport, the Scott County seat, stands on the Mississippi at Iowa's eastern edge. It belongs to the Quad Cities, a group of five that also takes in Bettendorf in Iowa and Rock Island, Moline and East Moline in Illinois. The metro area holds 381,801 people.

The city spreads over about 66 square miles at 660 feet. The river runs east to west here and the ground climbs toward the north. Population has hovered near 100,000 for roughly four decades, so a seller should not count on a rush of new arrivals. Condition and price carry the sale.

  • Vander Veer Park Historic District: anchored by Vander Veer Park, which was modeled on New York's Central Park.
  • Village of East Davenport: its Lindsay Park served as a Civil War parade ground for Camp McClellan.

Sioux City in brief

Sioux City is the Woodbury County seat, at the far northwest corner of Iowa, close to the South Dakota and Nebraska lines. The Missouri River is the city's western edge, and a slice of town extends into Plymouth County. The 2020 census counted 85,797 residents, the fourth-largest city in Iowa, with 144,334 people in the metro area.

Buyers and renters come from across the tri-state area, not only from inside the city limits. Median household income is $74,972 and the median age is 34.7. Tyson Fresh Meats, with about 4,500 employees, Seaboard Triumph Foods and the Sioux City Community School District lead the local job list, and many owners here also hold a rental or two.

Older houses and what inspectors flag

The city was founded in 1854 and incorporated on January 16, 1857, so much of the housing is old. Rose Hill has large, century-old houses. The Heights has estates built from the 1890s to the 1940s, including Prairie School homes. Morningside began as a late-19th-century streetcar suburb on hilly ground, and Indian Hills was built between the 1960s and the 1980s.

A house from the older eras can carry original plumbing, plaster walls or an older foundation, and an inspector hired by a buyer will write those up first. An owner unwilling to fund that work might look at selling as-is.

Condition varies block by block, but the neighborhoods differ in character and house type.

  • Riverside: flat, blue-collar area on the Big Sioux River floodplain.
  • Leeds: mostly residential, with north-south streets named for presidents.
  • Kelly Park: blue-collar residential area around the municipal park.
  • Prospect Hill: one of the oldest residential areas, walkable to downtown.
  • Southern Hills: the newest part of Morningside, anchored by Southern Hills Mall.
  • Woodbury Heights: newer hillside development off Fieldcrest Drive.

Newer hillside and Morningside homes usually need less structural work than a 1910 house near the river. The reverse happens too, when a long-time owner stopped maintaining a newer home.

Flood zones and the Missouri River

Homes close to the Missouri or the Big Sioux can run into flood questions. The Missouri reached 35.25 feet at Sioux City on July 21, 2011, more than four feet above the previous high set in 1984. That event closed Interstate 29 for about two months, and the 2019 Midwest floods closed a long stretch of the interstate south of here.

A house inside a mapped flood zone prompts requests from buyers and their lenders for an elevation certificate or an insurance quote. A cash buyer needs no lender, so that step usually drops out of the timeline.

Coralville borders the city to the northwest, and University Heights lies entirely inside the city limits.

Flood risk is real in parts of Iowa City, and the 2008 flood is the event buyers remember. Water passed the Coralville Reservoir's emergency spillway on June 11, 2008, and the Iowa River crested at a record 30.46 feet on June 13. Nineteen campus buildings were damaged.

The city requires a floodplain development permit in addition to a building permit for work in a flood hazard area. An elevation certificate is needed when a new structure is finished, when a remodel or repair costs 50 percent or more of the building's value, or when an addition increases floor area by 25 percent or more. New buildings must sit one foot above the 0.2 percent flood elevation.

The maps have changed too. New FEMA maps took effect in August 2025. Flood heights dropped along Ralston Creek, which could take some properties out of the high-risk zone, and rose along Willow Creek, which could add some. Buildings in the 1 percent zone need flood insurance if the loan is federally backed. Because the city takes part in the Community Rating System, policies there get an automatic 20 percent discount.

Factory work built this city. The settlement began as Prairie Rapids Crossing in 1845 and became Waterloo when Charles Mullan petitioned for a post office. The city incorporated in 1868, and population jumped from 8,490 in 1895 to 33,097 in 1915. The Waterloo Gasoline Engine Company began making Waterloo Boy tractors in 1893, and Rath Packing arrived in the same period. Much of the older housing traces to those decades.

The boom did not hold evenly. John Deere cut about 10,000 jobs in the 1980s farm recession and now employs roughly a third of its peak workforce, with more layoffs in 2024 and 2025.
